cs-u3-negation.description: Negate nested specifications without losing scope and identify the evidence needed to refute them.

cs-u4-sets.description: Distinguish membership, inclusion, empty sets and sets of subsets.

cs-u4-sequences.description: Model ordered records correctly and separate a tuple from a set of possible tuples.

cs-u4-relations.description: Classify relations by their incoming and outgoing pairs, keeping endpoints explicit.

cs-u4-images.title: Images, inverse images and inverse relations
cs-u4-images.description: Find images and preimages without confusing an inverse relation with an inverse function.

cs-u4-cardinality.title: Finite cardinality and reversible encodings
cs-u4-cardinality.description: Use injections, surjections, bijections and subset encodings to compare finite sizes.

cs-u5-bounds.title: Induction for exponential bounds
cs-u5-bounds.description: Verify the algebra and starting range of an inductive inequality.

cs-u5-strengthening.title: Strengthening the induction hypothesis
cs-u5-strengthening.description: Strengthen a claim just enough to preserve the information needed by the next step.

cs-u5-strong.title: Strong induction for smaller subproblems
cs-u5-strong.description: Use all smaller established cases while checking decrease and domain membership.

cs-u5-bases.title: Multiple base cases and dependency gaps
cs-u5-bases.description: Choose enough bases to support every dependency and detect missing links in a proof.

cs-u5-principles.title: Induction, well-ordering and proof review
cs-u5-principles.description: Relate the three proof principles and diagnose a complete induction argument.

cs-u6-invariants.title: Prove a resource invariant
cs-u6-invariants.description: Check initialization and preservation, and identify what an invariant does and does not prove.

cs-u6-partial-correctness.title: From a loop invariant to the result
cs-u6-partial-correctness.description: Use a loop invariant and an exit condition to prove partial correctness; repair an update that breaks the proof.

cs-u6-termination.title: Termination needs a well-founded decrease
cs-u6-termination.description: Choose a decreasing measure with the correct domain, and distinguish safety, partial correctness and total correctness.

cs-u6-matching-trace.description: Find a blocking pair and trace deferred acceptance under explicit preference assumptions.

cs-u6-matching-proof.title: Why deferred acceptance works
cs-u6-matching-proof.description: Use a finite proposal count and a monotonic preference invariant to justify termination and stability.

cs-u7-recursive-definitions.description: Read constructors as exact mathematical rules and evaluate a function by following the structure.

cs-u7-structural-induction.title: Prove properties of every tree
cs-u7-structural-induction.description: Use the actual constructors in an induction proof and reject circular reasoning.

cs-u7-brackets.title: Balanced brackets and unique decomposition
cs-u7-brackets.description: Check every prefix, identify the recursive decomposition, and detect an ambiguous recursive function.

cs-u7-recursive-functions.description: Distinguish a terminating recursive algorithm, an underdetermined equation and incompatible cases.

cs-u7-expressions.title: Expression trees and semantics-preserving rewrites
cs-u7-expressions.description: Separate syntax from value and justify a recursive transformation by its constructor cases.

cs-u7-finite-games.title: Recursive reasoning about winning moves
cs-u7-finite-games.description: Classify finite game positions by their successors and prove a strategy rather than merely finding a lucky play.

cs-u7-search-trees.title: Search trees: global invariants and cost
cs-u7-search-trees.description: Check the full search-tree condition and connect correctness and search cost to recursive structure.

cs-u8-bijections.title: Compare infinite sets by explicit maps
cs-u8-bijections.description: Check injectivity and surjectivity separately and construct a correspondence with N.

cs-u8-enumeration.description: Design enumerations that reach each object after finitely many steps, and diagnose starvation.

cs-u8-diagonal.title: Build the missing infinite sequence
cs-u8-diagonal.description: Execute a diagonal construction and identify the quantifier that makes it an impossibility proof.

cs-u8-power-sets.title: Cantor’s theorem and the limits of counting programs
cs-u8-power-sets.description: Construct a subset omitted by a proposed map and connect cardinality to the existence of undecidable languages.

cs-u8-halting.title: Halting, recognition and bounded questions
cs-u8-halting.description: Follow the self-reference contradiction, distinguish timeout from nontermination, and combine two recognizers.

cs-u8-set-foundations.title: Safe set formation and Russell’s paradox
cs-u8-set-foundations.description: Identify unrestricted set formation, derive the contradiction and distinguish an axiom-system repair from a consistency proof.

cs-statements.title: What counts as a statement?
cs-statements.body: A proposition is a statement with a definite truth value: true or false. It can be false and still be a proposition.
exampleSteps: It makes a definite claim.
That claim is false, but its truth value is clear.
cs-statements.takeaway: A question or instruction is not a proposition. A claim with an unspecified variable may need more information.

cs-implication.title: When does a rule fail?
cs-implication.body: An implication says: if P is true, Q must be true. To disprove it, find a case where P is true and Q is false.
cs-implication.example: If a number is divisible by 4, it is even.
exampleSteps: 8 is divisible by 4 and is even.
An odd number does not break this rule: its “if” condition is false.
cs-implication.takeaway: A counterexample makes P true and Q false.

cs-converse.title: Can you reverse a rule?
cs-converse.body: The converse swaps a rule’s condition and conclusion. A rule can be true while its converse is false.
cs-converse.example: If a number is divisible by 10, it is divisible by 5.
exampleSteps: The converse says: if divisible by 5, then divisible by 10.
15 satisfies the converse’s condition but not its conclusion.
cs-converse.takeaway: Reversing an implication creates a new claim that needs its own justification.

cs-negation.title: Negate a claim precisely
cs-negation.body: The negation of a claim is true exactly when the original claim is false. To disprove “every”, one exception is enough.
cs-negation.example: Every item in this list is positive.
exampleSteps: Its negation is: at least one item is not positive.
Not positive means zero or negative, not just negative.

ml-components.title: Read a vector
ml-components.body: A vector is an ordered list of numbers. Each component describes one coordinate or feature, and its position matters.
exampleSteps: The first component is 2; the second is −1.
There are three components, so x belongs to a 3-dimensional space.
ml-components.takeaway: Match the component order when comparing vectors or applying model weights.

ml-dot.title: Multiply, then add
ml-dot.body: The dot product multiplies matching components and adds the results. Both vectors must have the same number of components.
exampleSteps: Multiply matching entries: 2 × 3 = 6 and 1 × (−1) = −1.
Add them: a · b = 6 − 1 = 5.
ml-dot.takeaway: The dot product returns one number, not another vector.

ml-angle.title: What does the sign tell you?
ml-angle.body: For two nonzero vectors, the dot product’s sign tells you whether the angle between them is below, equal to, or above 90°.
exampleSteps: Their dot product is 0.
Both vectors are nonzero, so they are perpendicular.
ml-angle.takeaway: Positive: below 90°. Zero: 90°. Negative: above 90°. The angle with a zero vector is undefined.

ml-projection.title: Measure along a direction
ml-projection.body: The dot product with a unit vector gives a signed scalar projection: how much a vector points along that direction.
ml-projection.example: Let x = (3, 4) and unit direction u = (1, 0).
exampleSteps: The signed amount along the horizontal direction is 3.
ml-projection.takeaway: Use a unit direction. A negative projection means the opposite direction.

cs-u1-claims.title: Precise claims and assumptions
cs-u1-claims.body: A predicate becomes true or false when its inputs are fixed. A universal claim concerns every permitted input: one counterexample disproves it, while successful examples alone do not prove it. Unless stated otherwise, arithmetic uses mathematical integers without overflow; ℕ = {0, 1, 2, …}.
cs-u1-claims.example: For an array of length n, P(i, n) describes a valid index.
exampleSteps: P(2, 5) is true because 0 ≤ 2 < 5.
An implication P ⇒ Q lets us conclude Q once P has been established.
cs-u1-claims.takeaway: Check the input domain and the assumptions behind a claim.

cs-u1-direct.title: Direct proofs
cs-u1-direct.body: To prove an implication directly, assume its premise and derive its conclusion using definitions and established facts. Make the assumptions supporting each step explicit.
cs-u1-direct.example: If a = 4k for an integer k, then a + 4 is also a multiple of 4.
exampleSteps: Since k + 1 is an integer, this is an integer multiple of 4.
cs-u1-direct.takeaway: A direct proof connects the premise to the conclusion through justified steps.

cs-u1-contrapositive.title: Converses and contrapositives
cs-u1-contrapositive.body: P ⇒ Q is equivalent to its contrapositive, ¬Q ⇒ ¬P. Reversing it to Q ⇒ P produces the converse, which needs its own justification.
cs-u1-contrapositive.example: A multiple of 10 is a multiple of 5.
exampleSteps: Its contrapositive says: a number not divisible by 5 cannot be divisible by 10.
The converse is different: 5 is divisible by 5 but not by 10.
cs-u1-contrapositive.takeaway: For a contrapositive, negate both statements and reverse their order.

cs-u1-equivalence.title: If and only if
cs-u1-equivalence.body: Proving P ⇔ Q requires both directions. Alternatively, connect the statements through steps that are all reversible.
cs-u1-equivalence.formula: P ⇔ Q: P ⇒ Q and Q ⇒ P
exampleSteps: Subtracting 5 gives x = 4.
Adding 5 reverses the step and gives x + 5 = 9.
cs-u1-equivalence.takeaway: One implication alone does not establish an equivalence.

cs-u1-cases.title: Proof by cases
cs-u1-cases.body: Split the permitted inputs into cases that cover every possibility. Prove the claim in each case; check boundaries carefully.
cs-u1-cases.example: To prove |x| ≥ 0 for real x, split by the sign of x.
exampleSteps: If x ≥ 0, then |x| = x ≥ 0.
If x < 0, then |x| = −x > 0.
cs-u1-cases.takeaway: Correct arguments within incomplete cases do not prove the whole claim.

cs-u1-contradiction.title: Contradiction and proof review
cs-u1-contradiction.body: A contradiction proof assumes the claim is false and derives something impossible. When reviewing any proof, check for circular reasoning and assumptions that do not match the problem.
cs-u1-contradiction.example: A positive real x cannot satisfy x + 1 ≤ x.
exampleSteps: Assume x + 1 ≤ x.
Subtracting x gives 1 ≤ 0, which is impossible.
cs-u1-contradiction.takeaway: A proof must establish its claim under the assumptions of the actual problem.

cs-u2-ordering.title: What well-ordering guarantees
cs-u2-ordering.body: Every nonempty subset of ℕ has a least element. A set is well-ordered when every nonempty subset has a least element. A lower bound need not belong to the set; a minimum must. Throughout this unit, sets use the usual numerical order.
exampleSteps: Three belongs to the set and is no larger than any other member.
Finiteness is not required.
cs-u2-ordering.takeaway: Having a minimum is different from every nonempty subset having a minimum.

cs-u2-minimal.title: The smallest counterexample
cs-u2-minimal.body: To establish P(n) for all n ∈ ℕ, suppose counterexamples exist and choose the smallest one. Derive a contradiction, either by proving it satisfies P, or by finding a smaller counterexample.
cs-u2-minimal.example: If P(0) is already established, a smallest counterexample must be positive.
exampleSteps: Let m be the smallest counterexample.
Every permitted value smaller than m satisfies P.
cs-u2-minimal.takeaway: A smaller value contradicts minimality only if it is also a counterexample.

cs-u2-correctness.title: Proving a counting function correct
cs-u2-correctness.body: Consider a function on finite binary strings. It returns 0 for the empty string; on a prefix followed by bit b, it returns countOnes(prefix) + b. Here b has numerical value 0 or 1. We will prove correctness using the length of a shortest failing input.
exampleSteps: countOnes("") = 0
countOnes(prefix followed by bit b) = countOnes(prefix) + b
cs-u2-correctness.takeaway: Choose the smallest failing length, so every shorter input is handled correctly.

cs-u2-factors.title: Existence of prime factorizations
cs-u2-factors.body: A prime is an integer greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. We will use a smallest-counterexample argument to show that every integer greater than 1 is a product of primes. A single prime counts as such a product.
cs-u2-factors.example: This expression writes 42 as a product of primes.
exampleSteps: Each factor is prime.
A prime such as 7 is already a one-factor product of primes.
cs-u2-factors.takeaway: Existence and uniqueness are separate claims.

cs-u2-termination.title: Well-ordering and termination
cs-u2-termination.body: A computation cannot keep strictly decreasing a nonnegative integer forever. A termination argument therefore looks for such a measure. Assume each individual loop iteration finishes; a measure that merely stays the same or decreases is insufficient by itself.
cs-u2-termination.formula: V ∈ ℕ; each step strictly lowers V
cs-u2-termination.example: Removing one item per iteration from a fixed finite queue decreases its remaining length.
exampleSteps: The length is a nonnegative integer.
It decreases by 1 each time an item is removed.
cs-u2-termination.takeaway: The measure’s domain and strict decrease both matter.

cs-u3-conditions.title: Boolean conditions and specifications
cs-u3-conditions.body: AND requires both operands; inclusive OR permits either or both. XOR requires exactly one. P ⇒ Q fails only when P is true and Q is false; it does not assert causation or the converse. P ⇔ Q requires equal truth values. Here all Boolean checks are defined, deterministic and have no side effects. Logical equivalence alone does not justify reordering real code that can throw, mutate state or fail to terminate.
cs-u3-conditions.example: A job may run exactly when capacity C is available and either token T or override O is present: C ∧ (T ∨ O). With C=true, T=false and O=true, the condition is true.
cs-u3-conditions.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a requirement, its converse and an implementation condition.

cs-u3-equivalence.title: Equivalence and Boolean algebra
cs-u3-equivalence.body: Equivalent formulas agree on every assignment. A valid formula is true on every assignment; a satisfiable formula is true on at least one. To disprove equivalence, one differing assignment suffices. Useful laws include ¬(P ∧ Q) ≡ ¬P ∨ ¬Q, ¬(P ∨ Q) ≡ ¬P ∧ ¬Q, and P ⇒ Q ≡ ¬P ∨ Q. The symbol ≡ here means equivalence across assignments, not an extra program operator.
cs-u3-equivalence.example: ¬(Ready ∨ Busy) is equivalent to ¬Ready ∧ ¬Busy: both original flags must be false. Checking just one assignment would not establish this equivalence.
cs-u3-equivalence.takeaway: The learner can justify simplification by a law or a complete truth table.

cs-u3-normal-forms.title: Truth tables and normal forms
cs-u3-normal-forms.body: A literal is a Boolean variable or its negation. DNF is an OR of terms, each an AND of literals. CNF is an AND of clauses, each an OR of literals. To build a full DNF over fixed variables, write one term for each true row, mentioning every variable with the sign that selects that row. An n-variable truth table has 2^n rows. Form conversion can expand a short formula substantially.
cs-u3-normal-forms.example: For variables X,Y, a formula true only at (true,false) has full DNF X ∧ ¬Y. If (false,true) is also a true row, add the term ¬X ∧ Y using OR.
cs-u3-normal-forms.takeaway: The learner can connect a formula representation to its complete set of satisfying rows.

cs-u3-sat.title: SAT as a consistency check
cs-u3-sat.body: SAT asks whether there is any assignment making a propositional formula true. For constraints joined by AND, one assignment must satisfy every constraint simultaneously. A witness proves satisfiability; one failed trial does not prove impossibility. Unsatisfiability needs an exhaustive finite check or a valid argument. F is valid exactly when ¬F is unsatisfiable. A witness can be checked by evaluating the formula; finding one is a different task.
cs-u3-sat.example: Constraints K ⇒ L and K ∧ ¬L cannot both hold: the second makes K true and L false, which violates the first. This contradiction proves the conjunction unsatisfiable.
cs-u3-sat.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a witness, a failed trial, and an impossibility argument.

cs-u3-quantifiers.title: Predicates, domains and quantifiers
cs-u3-quantifiers.body: A predicate becomes a truth-valued claim once its free variables are assigned or quantified. ∀x∈D means every element of D; ∃x∈D means at least one, not exactly one. A restricted universal usually uses implication: ∀x∈D (Eligible(x) ⇒ Ready(x)). A restricted existential uses conjunction: ∃x∈D (Eligible(x) ∧ Ready(x)). For an explicitly empty D, the universal is true and the existential false. As in the book, an omitted discourse domain is assumed nonempty.
cs-u3-quantifiers.example: If Jobs={j1,j2} and only j2 is queued, “some job is queued” is true with witness j2. “Every job is queued” is false with counterexample j1.
cs-u3-quantifiers.takeaway: The learner can state the domain and distinguish a witness from a universal guarantee.

cs-u3-nested.title: Quantifier order and dependent witnesses
cs-u3-nested.body: In ∀x∈A ∃y∈B R(x,y), the chosen y may depend on x. In ∃y∈B ∀x∈A R(x,y), one y must work for every x. A common witness gives a per-input witness, but the converse need not hold. Swapping two universal quantifiers or two existential quantifiers preserves meaning; swapping different kinds generally does not. Parentheses and domains make the scope explicit.
cs-u3-nested.example: Two files f1,f2 have separate replicas: R(f1,s1) and R(f2,s2), with no other replica pairs. Every file has a server, but no single server stores both files.
cs-u3-nested.takeaway: The learner can test a quantifier claim against a small relation rather than rely on ambiguous English.

cs-u3-negation.title: Negating specifications and finding countermodels
cs-u3-negation.body: Negation swaps ∀ and ∃ and negates the predicate: ¬∀x P(x) ≡ ∃x ¬P(x), and ¬∃x P(x) ≡ ∀x ¬P(x). Apply this one quantifier at a time. Negating an implication gives a true premise and false conclusion. A formula with predicates is valid only if it holds for every allowed domain and interpretation; a single countermodel refutes validity.
cs-u3-negation.example: Negating “Every client has an available route” gives “Some client has no available route”: ¬[∀c∈C ∃r∈R A(c,r)] ≡ ∃c∈C ∀r∈R ¬A(c,r).
cs-u3-negation.takeaway: The learner can describe the exact witness or countermodel required by a failed specification.

cs-u4-sets.title: Sets, membership and exact collections
cs-u4-sets.body: A set ignores order and repeated listings. x∈A means x is an element; B⊆A means every element of B belongs to A. The empty set ∅ is a subset of every set. The set {∅} has one element and is not empty. Set-builder notation {x∈D | P(x)} filters a domain by a predicate. The power set pow(A) contains all subsets of A, including ∅ and A itself.
cs-u4-sets.example: If Flags={read,write}, then {read}⊆Flags and {read}∈pow(Flags). The string read is an element of Flags; the singleton set {read} is a different object.
cs-u4-sets.takeaway: The learner avoids element/subset and empty-container errors before manipulating collections.

cs-u4-set-algebra.title: Set operations and membership proofs
cs-u4-set-algebra.body: Union ∪ corresponds to OR of membership; intersection ∩ to AND. A\B contains elements of A absent from B. A complement must name its universe U: U\A. To prove A=B, show that an arbitrary x belongs to A iff it belongs to B, or prove both inclusions. One-sided inclusion does not establish equality. Logic operates on truth values; set operations operate on sets.
cs-u4-set-algebra.example: With U={a,b,c,d}, A={a,b} and B={b,c}, A∩B={b}, A\B={a}, and U\(A∪B)={d}.
cs-u4-set-algebra.takeaway: The learner connects Unit 3 logic to typed set reasoning and can exhibit a failing element.

cs-u4-sequences.title: Sequences, tuples and Cartesian products
cs-u4-sequences.body: A sequence preserves order and repetitions. A tuple is a finite sequence; equal tuples have the same length and equal components at each position. A×B is the set of ordered pairs (a,b) with a∈A and b∈B. It is usually different from B×A. S^n contains length-n sequences over S. S^0 contains one sequence, the empty sequence, even when S is empty.
cs-u4-sequences.example: For Method={GET,POST} and Status={200,500}, Method×Status has four pairs. (GET,500) is one pair, not the whole product; reversing it gives a differently typed record.
cs-u4-sequences.takeaway: The learner can reason about product types without losing order, multiplicity or the empty case.

cs-u4-functions.title: Functions, support and composition
cs-u4-functions.body: Following this edition, f:A→B may be partial: each a has at most one value in B. Its support contains inputs where it is defined; f is total when support(f)=A. Its range contains values actually produced, which may be fewer than the codomain B. Composition applies the right-hand function first: (g∘f)(x)=g(f(x)). For partial functions it is defined only if f(x) exists and belongs to support(g).
cs-u4-functions.example: Let f:Z→Z be f(x)=x+2 and g:Z→Z be g(x)=3x, both total. Then (g∘f)(1)=9 whereas (f∘g)(1)=5. Order matters.
cs-u4-functions.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a declared input type from supported inputs and actually produced outputs.

cs-u4-relations.title: Relations and mapping properties
cs-u4-relations.body: A relation from A to B specifies a graph contained in A×B. It may relate one input to several outputs. Functional means at most one output per input; total means at least one. Injective means at most one input per output, and surjective means at least one. In the book these properties also apply to relations that are not functions. A bijection has exactly one output per input and exactly one input per output. Changing A or B can change these properties.
cs-u4-relations.example: From A={p,q} to B={1,2,3}, graph {(p,1),(q,2)} is a total injective function, but not surjective because 3 is not reached.
cs-u4-relations.takeaway: The learner classifies mappings using all declared endpoints, including isolated ones.

cs-u4-images.title: Images, inverse images and inverse relations
cs-u4-images.body: For a relation R:A→B, R(S) collects outputs related to some input in S⊆A. The inverse relation R^(-1) reverses every pair. Its image R^(-1)(T) collects inputs related to some output in T⊆B: the inverse image, or preimage. This is defined even if R is not bijective. For a function, its inverse relation is functional exactly when the original function is injective; it is a total inverse function on B when the original is a bijection.
cs-u4-images.example: If f(a)=red, f(b)=red and f(c)=blue, then f({a,c})={red,blue} and f^(-1)({red})={a,b}. There is no unique inverse value at red, but its preimage set is perfectly defined.
cs-u4-images.takeaway: The learner can query mappings in either direction while preserving single-valuedness constraints.

cs-u4-cardinality.title: Finite cardinality and reversible encodings
cs-u4-cardinality.body: For finite sets, a total injective function A→B requires |A|≤|B|; a surjective function requires |A|≥|B|. A bijection proves equal sizes. If |A|=|B| and f is total, injectivity and surjectivity are equivalent. Totality matters: a partial injection can leave inputs unsupported. For a fixed ordered list of n distinct elements, each subset corresponds to its n-bit membership vector, so the power set has 2^n members.
cs-u4-cardinality.example: For ordered fields (id,name,age), subset {id,age} corresponds to vector (1,0,1). Every subset has one vector and every vector specifies one subset, giving a bijection.
cs-u4-cardinality.takeaway: The learner can justify finite size claims and explain when a collision-free encoding is impossible.

cs-u5-ordinary.title: Ordinary induction and the proof contract
cs-u5-ordinary.body: To prove P(n) for every integer n≥n0, establish P(n0), then fix an arbitrary k≥n0 and prove P(k)⇒P(k+1). In the step, P(k) is a temporary assumption for proving an implication; assuming P(k+1) would be circular. The argument must work for every allowed k. An empty sum is 0. Induction verifies a proposed formula; it does not automatically discover one.
cs-u5-ordinary.example: A buffer begins with capacity C(0)=5 and grows by 3 each step: C(n+1)=C(n)+3. Claim C(n)=5+3n. Base: C(0)=5. Step: assuming C(k)=5+3k gives C(k+1)=5+3k+3=5+3(k+1).
cs-u5-ordinary.takeaway: The learner can identify the base, hypothesis, target and quantification of a valid induction proof.

cs-u5-bounds.title: Induction for exponential bounds
cs-u5-bounds.body: An inequality proof needs a bridge from the bound available at k to the bound required at k+1. Multiplying by a positive quantity preserves direction; a negative multiplier reverses it. Verify the bridge on the entire induction range. A true base and a failed proof strategy do not establish that the theorem is false. Use exact mathematical integers here, without overflow.
cs-u5-bounds.example: To prove 2^n≥n+1 for n≥0: the base is 1≥1. If 2^k≥k+1, then 2^(k+1)≥2(k+1)≥k+2 because k≥0. The final expression is the next target.
cs-u5-bounds.takeaway: The learner can distinguish a numerical base check from the range condition supporting a general step.

cs-u5-strengthening.title: Strengthening the induction hypothesis
cs-u5-strengthening.body: A weak induction hypothesis may omit information needed to advance. Prove a stronger predicate Q(n) that implies the original goal, with its own base and step. Stronger must still be true. A common engineering pattern is a coupled update: proving a property of one quantity requires tracking a second quantity. Strengthening the predicate is different from strong induction, which allows earlier indices.
cs-u5-strengthening.example: Let u(0)=1, v(0)=2, u(n+1)=u(n)+v(n), and v(n+1)=2u(n)+v(n). To prove u(n)>0, use the stronger claim u(n)>0 and v(n)>0. Both updated values are then positive; tracking u alone does not directly bound v.
cs-u5-strengthening.takeaway: The learner can choose a useful auxiliary fact and check that it is established, not merely assumed.

cs-u5-strong.title: Strong induction for smaller subproblems
cs-u5-strong.body: Strong induction for n≥n0 permits assuming P(j) for every n0≤j<n when proving P(n). This helps when a subproblem is smaller but not exactly n-1. Every use of the hypothesis must satisfy that range. Handle terminal inputs explicitly. All arithmetic is exact, floor(x) is the greatest integer ≤x, and the integer recursions here are distinct from structural induction, reserved for Unit 7.
cs-u5-strong.example: For n≥1, a procedure stops at n=1 and otherwise recurses on floor(n/2). For n≥2, 1≤floor(n/2)<n. Strong induction therefore proves termination: the recursive call is covered by a smaller terminating case.
cs-u5-strong.takeaway: The learner can apply the induction hypothesis only to legitimate smaller inputs.

cs-u5-bases.title: Multiple base cases and dependency gaps
cs-u5-bases.body: A recurrence using n-2 and n-3 needs enough directly established cases before both dependencies lie in range. Likewise, a step P(k)⇒P(k+d) only moves within a residue class modulo d; one base may leave whole classes uncovered. The number of bases is determined by the proof’s dependencies and starting range, not a universal rule. Inspect the earliest inductive transition carefully.
cs-u5-bases.example: If P(k)⇒P(k+3) for every k≥0, proving P(0), P(1) and P(2) starts all three chains: 0,3,6,...; 1,4,7,...; and 2,5,8,.... P(0) alone starts only the first chain.
cs-u5-bases.takeaway: The learner can explain why base coverage is sufficient instead of checking an arbitrary number of examples.

cs-u5-principles.title: Induction, well-ordering and proof review
cs-u5-principles.body: Ordinary induction, strong induction and well-ordering over the nonnegative integers have equivalent proving power. To package strong induction as ordinary induction, use Q(n): “P(j) holds for every 0≤j≤n.” Conversely, if a base and successor step hold but a counterexample exists, well-ordering gives a least counterexample m. The base excludes m=0, so P(m-1) and the step force P(m), a contradiction. Equivalence of methods does not repair a missing premise.
cs-u5-principles.example: Suppose P(0) and every successor implication hold. A least failing index m cannot be 0. Minimality gives P(m-1); the successor implication then gives P(m). Thus no failing index exists.
cs-u5-principles.takeaway: The learner can audit an induction proof and connect it to minimal-counterexample reasoning.

cs-u6-model.title: States, transitions and reachability
cs-u6-model.body: A state records the information needed to determine which transitions are allowed. An execution starts in an initial state and follows allowed transitions. A state is reachable if some finite execution reaches it, including the execution with zero transitions. Nondeterminism allows several next states. One successful execution establishes possibility; a guarantee must cover every allowed execution. State updates here are atomic and use old values on their right-hand sides.
cs-u6-model.example: A worker has state (q,d), with q pending tasks and d completed tasks. Starting at (3,0), the rule (q,d) → (q-1,d+1), allowed only for q>0, gives (3,0) → (2,1) → (1,2) → (0,3).
cs-u6-model.takeaway: Can the learner give an allowed trace and identify the quantifier in a reachability or correctness claim?

cs-u6-invariants.title: Prove a resource invariant
cs-u6-invariants.body: To use the Invariant Principle, choose a predicate I that holds initially and prove I(s) implies I(t) for every allowed transition s→t. Then I holds in every reachable state. The book calls the transition property a preserved invariant: its preservation proof must cover every I-state in the declared state space, including unreachable ones. An invariant gives a necessary condition for reachability, not generally a sufficient condition.
cs-u6-invariants.example: For a pool with state (free,busy)∈N², allocation changes (f,b) to (f-1,b+1) when f>0. Returning a resource changes it to (f+1,b-1) when b>0. Starting with capacity C, both updates preserve f+b=C.
cs-u6-invariants.takeaway: Can the learner verify both proof obligations and distinguish safety from reachability?

cs-u6-partial-correctness.title: From a loop invariant to the result
cs-u6-partial-correctness.body: Partial correctness means: for every permitted input, if execution terminates, the output satisfies the specification. It does not claim termination. At loop boundaries, establish an invariant, show each complete iteration preserves it, then combine it with the exit condition. Exact arithmetic and explicit update order matter. For repeated addition, an accumulator can record work already done while a counter records work still to do.
cs-u6-partial-correctness.example: To compute a product a·n for a,n∈N, initialize (i,s)=(0,0) and repeat (i,s)→(i+1,s+a) while i<n. The predicate s=a·i and 0≤i≤n holds initially and is preserved. On exit i=n, so s=a·n.
cs-u6-partial-correctness.takeaway: Can the learner supply the missing algebraic step and separate partial correctness from termination?

cs-u6-termination.title: Termination needs a well-founded decrease
cs-u6-termination.body: A nonnegative integer-valued measure that strictly decreases on every transition rules out infinite executions. From measure r, there can be at most r such transitions. Weak decrease allows infinite repetitions. Strict decrease in the nonnegative reals is also insufficient: 1,1/2,1/4,... never reaches 0. Partial correctness plus termination gives total correctness for the stated inputs.
cs-u6-termination.example: For a loop with integer 0≤i≤n and update i′=i+1 when i<n, use r=n-i. The guard ensures r≥1 before a step and r′=r-1≥0 afterwards. Therefore the loop terminates.
cs-u6-termination.takeaway: Can the learner reject a plausible-looking termination argument by constructing an infinite execution?

cs-u6-matching-trace.title: Stable matching: trace and challenge a result
cs-u6-matching-trace.body: Use two equally sized groups, applicants and teams, with one-to-one matching and strict complete rankings of the other group. An unmatched applicant-team pair blocks a matching if each prefers the other to its current partner. A stable matching has no blocking pair. In applicant-proposing deferred acceptance, a free applicant proposes to its highest-ranked team not yet tried; a team keeps its preferred applicant among its current hold and new proposals and rejects the rest.
cs-u6-matching-trace.example: If T holds B and prefers A to B, a proposal from A makes T hold A and reject B. The hold is tentative: B can continue proposing. Preference ranks, not proposal arrival order, decide whom T keeps.
cs-u6-matching-trace.takeaway: Can the learner check both sides of a blocking pair and carry a rejection into the next step?

cs-u6-matching-proof.title: Why deferred acceptance works
cs-u6-matching-proof.body: In the strict, complete, equal-size one-to-one model, an applicant proposes to each team at most once, so at most n² proposals occur. A team that holds an applicant never becomes empty and can only replace its hold with someone it prefers. Thus every team that rejects A ends with someone it prefers to A. A free applicant cannot exhaust all teams: then all n teams would be holding applicants while one of the n applicants remained free. The resulting complete matching is stable. Proposer-optimal means best partner among stable matchings, not necessarily first choice overall.
cs-u6-matching-proof.example: If A prefers team T to its final partner, A must have proposed to T earlier and been rejected. T’s final partner is preferred by T to A, so A and T cannot block the final matching.
cs-u6-matching-proof.takeaway: Can the learner identify the invariant used in the stability argument and state the theorem’s assumptions?

cs-u7-recursive-definitions.title: Define finite structures precisely
cs-u7-recursive-definitions.body: A recursive data type is the smallest collection containing its base objects and closed under its constructors. “Smallest” excludes extra objects not obtained by finitely many constructor applications. For integer lists: [] is a list, and a::xs is a list when a∈Z and xs is a list. The constructor prepends a. A function can specify one base case and one rule per constructor, with recursive calls on the smaller components.
cs-u7-recursive-definitions.example: Define F([])=0 and F(a::xs)=a-F(xs). Then F(3::(8::[]))=3-(8-0)=-5. Unfolding the tail first prevents subtraction from being grouped incorrectly.
cs-u7-recursive-definitions.takeaway: Can the learner distinguish a valid finite object from an ill-typed or infinite expression and evaluate its recursive definition?

cs-u7-structural-induction.title: Prove properties of every tree
cs-u7-structural-induction.body: A finite full binary tree is either Leaf(v) or Join(L,R), where L and R are trees. Structural induction checks every leaf and proves the property for Join(L,R) assuming it for both children. Let leaves(T) count leaves and inner(T) count Join nodes. A leaf has counts (1,0); a join has leaves(L)+leaves(R) leaves and 1+inner(L)+inner(R) internal nodes. These rules prove leaves(T)=inner(T)+1.
cs-u7-structural-induction.example: At a join, substituting the two child hypotheses gives leaves(T)=(inner(L)+1)+(inner(R)+1)=inner(T)+1. The argument covers unequal subtree sizes; no balanced-tree assumption is used.
cs-u7-structural-induction.takeaway: Can the learner complete both constructor cases and identify exactly where each induction hypothesis is used?

cs-u7-brackets.title: Balanced brackets and unique decomposition
cs-u7-brackets.body: A parenthesis string is balanced exactly when its total balance is 0 and every prefix has nonnegative balance, counting “(” as +1 and “)” as -1. Recursively, the empty string ε is balanced; every nonempty balanced string has the unique form (s)t, where s and t are balanced and the first closing parenthesis matching the initial opening one determines the split. Equal total counts alone are insufficient. If alternative construction rules allow multiple derivations, a function on strings must give consistent values across all derivations.
cs-u7-brackets.example: For (()())(), the first opening parenthesis closes at position 6, so the unique decomposition (s)t has s=()() and t=(). Position numbering begins at 1.
cs-u7-brackets.takeaway: Can the learner find the first invalid prefix and explain why ambiguity can make a proposed function inconsistent?

cs-u7-recursive-functions.title: Well-defined recursion and shrinking inputs
cs-u7-recursive-functions.body: A base case alone does not make recursion valid. The cases must cover the domain consistently, and recursive evaluation must progress toward a base case. For h(0)=0 and h(n)=1+h(floor(n/2)) when n≥1, every recursive argument is a smaller nonnegative integer. Conversely, equations referring only to larger inputs may admit many mathematical solutions while their direct recursive implementation never returns. Mathematical simultaneous cases differ from an ordered if/else program.
cs-u7-recursive-functions.example: The recurrence h(0)=0; h(n)=1+h(floor(n/2)) gives h(9)=1+h(4)=2+h(2)=3+h(1)=4. This counts positive stages before reaching 0.
cs-u7-recursive-functions.takeaway: Can the learner state a decreasing argument and diagnose missing uniqueness or conflicting cases?

cs-u7-expressions.title: Expression trees and semantics-preserving rewrites
cs-u7-expressions.body: Expressions here are finite trees Const(k), Add(L,R), or Mul(L,R), with integer k. Evaluation is recursive: constants return k; Add sums child values; Mul multiplies them. Distinct trees can have equal values. Define mirror by leaving constants unchanged and swapping the recursively mirrored children at every Add or Mul. Structural induction proves eval(mirror(E))=eval(E), using commutativity for each operator. That argument needs revisiting if the language gains a noncommutative operator.
cs-u7-expressions.example: Add(Const(2),Const(5)) and Const(7) evaluate equally but are different syntax trees. A proof about evaluated values cannot silently conclude that the trees are identical.
cs-u7-expressions.takeaway: Can the learner trace a tree and identify the algebraic assumption behind a rewrite?

cs-u7-finite-games.title: Recursive reasoning about winning moves
cs-u7-finite-games.body: Consider a finite, perfect-information, two-player game without draws. Players alternate; a player with no legal move loses. A position is winning for the player to move iff it has some move to a losing position. It is losing iff every legal move leads to a winning position. Terminal positions are losing, since they have no legal moves. This recursive classification requires well-founded play; a reachable cycle cannot simply be treated as a finite game tree.
cs-u7-finite-games.example: If position U can move to V or W, and V is losing while W is winning for the next player, U is winning: choose V. Choosing W instead may lose, so “winning position” does not mean every move wins.
cs-u7-finite-games.takeaway: Can the learner choose a winning move and give a proof that covers the opponent’s possible replies?

cs-u7-search-trees.title: Search trees: global invariants and cost
cs-u7-search-trees.body: A binary search tree here stores distinct integer keys, one per nonempty node. Every key anywhere in the left subtree is smaller than the node key; every key in the right subtree is larger. Both subtrees satisfy the same rule. Checking only immediate children is insufficient. Inorder traversal returns left subtree keys, then the root, then right subtree keys. Search follows one branch per comparison. Its cost depends on height: a valid but skewed tree may require one comparison per stored key.
cs-u7-search-trees.example: With root 10, left child 4 and right child 15, searching for 15 compares first with 10 and then with 15. If a node 12 is placed inside the left subtree of 10, the root’s global bound is violated even when 12 is greater than its own parent.
cs-u7-search-trees.takeaway: Can the learner find an ancestor-bound violation and distinguish a valid tree from a balanced one?

cs-u8-bijections.title: Compare infinite sets by explicit maps
cs-u8-bijections.body: Two sets have the same cardinality when a bijection pairs their elements. Countably infinite means in bijection with N={0,1,2,...}; countable includes finite sets as well. An injection never merges different inputs. A surjection reaches every element of the declared codomain. Infinite sets can be in bijection with proper subsets, so conclusions valid only for finite sets must not be reused without their finiteness assumption.
cs-u8-bijections.example: The function f:N→{4n+2:n∈N}, f(n)=4n+2, is a bijection. Equal outputs imply equal inputs, and each target 4k+2 is reached by input k.
cs-u8-bijections.takeaway: Can the learner give both halves of a bijection proof and keep the codomain explicit?

cs-u8-enumeration.title: List finite strings, pairs and rationals
cs-u8-enumeration.body: All finite strings over a finite alphabet can be listed by increasing length, then lexicographically within each length. Each string then has only finitely many predecessors. For pairs (a,b)∈N², list by increasing a+b, then increasing a within each diagonal. Each diagonal is finite and every pair has a finite sum. This gives a listing of positive rationals by mapping (a,b) to (a+1)/(b+1); repeated values are allowed in a surjective listing or can be skipped.
cs-u8-enumeration.example: Over {a,b}, length-first order starts ε,a,b,aa,ab,ba,bb,aaa,... . Over N², diagonal order starts (0,0),(0,1),(1,0),(0,2),(1,1),(2,0),... . Neither method tries to finish an infinite block first.
cs-u8-enumeration.takeaway: Can the learner explain why an enumeration eventually reaches any chosen object?

cs-u8-diagonal.title: Build the missing infinite sequence
cs-u8-diagonal.body: Suppose someone lists infinite binary sequences s₀,s₁,s₂,... . Index bits from 0 and define d(n)=1-sₙ(n). For every row k, d differs from sₖ at bit k; therefore d is missing from that list. Since the list was arbitrary, no countable listing contains every infinite binary sequence. This proof concerns sequences, so it avoids ambiguities between different positional representations of the same real number. Finite binary strings remain countable.
cs-u8-diagonal.example: If the diagonal bits of the first four rows are 1,0,0,1, the first four bits of d are 0,1,1,0. These four differences illustrate the rule; the impossibility proof uses the rule at every natural-number index.
cs-u8-diagonal.takeaway: Can the learner construct the missing sequence and distinguish a finite illustration from the general proof?

cs-u8-power-sets.title: Cantor’s theorem and the limits of counting programs
cs-u8-power-sets.body: For any total function g:A→P(A), define D={a∈A:a∉g(a)}, where P(A) is the set of all subsets of A. If D=g(t), then t∈D iff t∉D, a contradiction. So no such g is surjective. The map a↦{a} is injective, which together gives |A|<|P(A)|. Finite program descriptions form a countable set; languages over a nonempty finite alphabet are subsets of its countably infinite set of finite strings. Cantor’s theorem makes this collection of languages uncountable.
cs-u8-power-sets.example: For A={u,v}, g(u)={u} and g(v)=∅ give D={v}: u is in g(u), while v is not in g(v). Neither output of g equals {v}.
cs-u8-power-sets.takeaway: Can the learner carry out the diagonal subset construction and state exactly what the counting argument establishes?

cs-u8-halting.title: Halting, recognition and bounded questions
cs-u8-halting.body: Programs in this mathematical model have finite descriptions and unbounded computation resources. A decider always halts with a correct yes/no answer. A recognizer for L halts and accepts every member of L; for a nonmember it may reject or run forever. Suppose H(p,x) always decides whether program p halts on input x. Define D(x): if H(x,x) says “halts”, loop forever; otherwise halt. Applying D to its own code contradicts H in either case. No universal H with all these guarantees exists.
cs-u8-halting.example: A simulation that has run for a million steps proves only that the program did not halt during those steps. In contrast, “Does it halt within t steps?” is decidable for any supplied finite t by bounded simulation.
cs-u8-halting.takeaway: Can the learner distinguish an impossible universal guarantee from useful restricted analyses?

cs-u8-set-foundations.title: Safe set formation and Russell’s paradox
cs-u8-set-foundations.body: Set-builder notation needs a legitimate ambient set. Separation forms {x∈A:P(x)} from an existing set A; it does not grant a set of every object satisfying an arbitrary property. If R were the set of all sets S with S∉S, substituting R would give R∈R iff R∉R. This rules out that unrestricted construction. Modern axioms restrict set formation. Avoiding this particular contradiction is not, by itself, a proof that the whole axiom system is consistent.
cs-u8-set-foundations.example: The set {n∈N:n²<10} is safely formed inside N and equals {0,1,2,3}. In contrast, writing “all sets” as the ambient collection cannot be assumed to define a set.
cs-u8-set-foundations.takeaway: Can the learner locate the invalid formation assumption without concluding that all ordinary set reasoning is contradictory?

cs-u9-divisibility.title: Divisibility and canonical remainders
cs-u9-divisibility.body: For a positive integer d and integer a, d|a means a=d·k for some k∈Z. If d divides a and b, it divides every integer linear combination r·a+s·b. A divisor of a product need not divide either factor individually; a prime divisor has a stronger property taught later. For a∈Z and positive n, Euclidean division gives unique integers q,r with a=qn+r and 0≤r<n. This draft always uses that nonnegative remainder convention.
cs-u9-divisibility.example: Dividing -23 by 5 gives -23=(-5)·5+2, so the quotient is -5 and the canonical remainder is 2. The expression (-4)·5-3 has a negative final term, so -3 is not the canonical remainder.
cs-u9-divisibility.takeaway: Can the learner exhibit the witness or counterexample behind each divisibility claim?

cs-u9-euclid.title: Euclid’s algorithm as a correctness proof
cs-u9-euclid.body: For nonnegative a,b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is their greatest positive common divisor. For b>0, writing a=qb+r gives gcd(a,b)=gcd(b,r): a divisor of a and b divides r=a-qb, and a divisor of b and r divides a=qb+r. Euclid repeatedly updates (x,y)→(y,x mod y) while y>0. The gcd is invariant; the new second coordinate is smaller than the old positive y. At y=0 the remaining x is the original gcd.
cs-u9-euclid.example: Starting from (78,30), the states are (30,18),(18,12),(12,6),(6,0). The invariant identifies 6 as the answer, and the decreasing second coordinate proves termination.
cs-u9-euclid.takeaway: Can the learner justify the algorithm rather than only execute it?

cs-u9-bezout.title: Extended Euclid and integer combinations
cs-u9-bezout.body: Extended Euclid tracks integer coefficients to express gcd(a,b)=u·a+v·b. Consequently a·x+b·y=c has integer solutions exactly when gcd(a,b)|c: every combination is divisible by the gcd, and a gcd representation can be scaled to any multiple. Coefficients may be negative. This theorem does not guarantee nonnegative solutions, which model a different constraint. A certificate g=u·a+v·b, together with g>0 and g|a,g|b, proves g is the gcd.
cs-u9-bezout.example: For 65 and 24: 65=2·24+17, 24=17+7, 17=2·7+3, 7=2·3+1. Back-substitution gives 1=19·24-7·65. The identity both certifies coprimality and supplies coefficients.
cs-u9-bezout.takeaway: Can the learner explain both directions of the integer-solvability criterion?

cs-u9-primes.title: Prime factors: use the hypotheses
cs-u9-primes.body: A prime is an integer greater than 1 with no positive divisors other than 1 and itself. Every integer greater than 1 has a prime factorization, unique up to order. If prime p divides ab, then p divides a or b; the word prime is essential. Gcds take the minimum exponent of each prime in the two factorizations. A composite n>1 has a prime divisor at most sqrt(n). To show there are infinitely many primes, a proposed finite complete list p₁,...,pₖ gives N=p₁...pₖ+1: none of those primes divides N, so a prime factor of N is missing.
cs-u9-primes.example: The gcd of 2⁴·3 and 2²·3² is 2²·3=12. In the infinitude argument, N need not itself be prime; the existence of a prime factor outside the proposed complete list is enough.
cs-u9-primes.takeaway: Can the learner distinguish the theorem from a stronger false statement suggested by its examples?

cs-u9-modular-arithmetic.title: Compute with residue classes
cs-u9-modular-arithmetic.body: For modulus n≥2, a≡b (mod n) means n|(a-b). It says the integers share a remainder, not that they are equal. Congruences can be added and multiplied; inputs and intermediate results may be replaced by their canonical remainders. Repeated squaring computes large powers by splitting the exponent into powers of 2 and reducing after each multiplication. Division requires additional conditions, developed in the next module.
cs-u9-modular-arithmetic.example: To compute 3⁵ mod 7: 3²≡2, 3⁴≡4, and 3⁵≡4·3≡5. Each reduced multiplication agrees with the full integer computation because congruence is preserved under multiplication.
cs-u9-modular-arithmetic.takeaway: Can the learner use modular equalities without confusing them with ordinary equality or unrestricted division?

cs-u9-inverses.title: When cancellation and inverses are valid
cs-u9-inverses.body: For n≥2, a has a multiplicative inverse modulo n exactly when gcd(a,n)=1. Extended Euclid supplies it from u·a+v·n=1. An invertible factor can be cancelled without changing the modulus. For ax≡b (mod n), let g=gcd(a,n). There are no solutions unless g|b. When it divides b, dividing a,b and n by g yields the equivalent congruence (a/g)x≡b/g (mod n/g). Dividing only the displayed coefficients while keeping n can lose solutions.
cs-u9-inverses.example: From 3·7-2·10=1, the inverse of 7 modulo 10 is 3. By contrast, 4x≡8 (mod 12) becomes x≡2 (mod 3), not x≡2 (mod 12).
cs-u9-inverses.takeaway: Can the learner explain the role of the gcd and avoid illegal cancellation?

cs-u9-euler.title: Euler’s theorem: check before reducing an exponent
cs-u9-euler.body: The totient φ(n) counts residues 0≤k<n with gcd(k,n)=1. For prime p and r≥1, φ(pʳ)=pʳ-pʳ⁻¹; for coprime a,b, φ(ab)=φ(a)φ(b). Euler’s theorem states a^φ(n)≡1 (mod n) when gcd(a,n)=1. Therefore exponents of such a can be reduced modulo φ(n). For prime p and p not dividing a, Fermat’s little theorem gives a^(p-1)≡1 (mod p). Passing one such congruence test does not prove the modulus prime.
cs-u9-euler.example: φ(20)=φ(4)φ(5)=2·4=8. Since gcd(3,20)=1, 3¹⁰≡3²≡9 modulo 20. The same exponent reduction cannot automatically be used for a=2, which is not coprime to 20.
cs-u9-euler.takeaway: Can the learner state and test the missing hypothesis before applying a powerful shortcut?

cs-u9-rsa.title: Toy RSA: assemble and audit the mathematics
cs-u9-rsa.body: For distinct primes p,q, let n=pq and φ(n)=(p-1)(q-1). Choose a positive exponent e coprime to φ(n), and positive d with ed≡1 modulo φ(n). The public pair is (n,e); encryption maps 0≤m<n to c=m^e mod n, and decryption computes c^d mod n. Euler directly proves recovery when gcd(m,n)=1. To cover all message residues, argue separately modulo p and q: a zero residue stays zero; a nonzero residue uses Fermat’s theorem. Agreement modulo both distinct primes implies agreement modulo their product. These small examples teach the arithmetic, not a deployable encryption design.
cs-u9-rsa.example: Take p=7, q=13. Then n=91 and φ(n)=72. With e=5, choose d=29 because 5·29=145=1+2·72. Thus encryption uses a fifth power and decryption a twenty-ninth power, both modulo 91.
cs-u9-rsa.takeaway: Can the learner identify each modulus and prove recovery without silently assuming the message is coprime to n?

ml-linear-regression.title: Linear regression: predictions and loss
ml-linear-regression.body:
Predict with y_hat = b + w^T x. A residual is prediction minus target: r_i = y_hat_i - y_i. For n examples, use L = (1/(2n)) sum_i r_i^2. This is half-MSE: the same minimizers as MSE, with half its gradient.

For an unregularized model, rescaling a feature to c*x preserves predictions when its weight becomes w/c (c != 0). Keep the bias unchanged. Dependent feature columns can give many optimal weight vectors; full column rank, including any bias column, makes the least-squares optimum unique.

Squared loss emphasizes large residuals. MAE = (1/n) sum_i |r_i| penalizes their absolute sizes. The two objectives can rank models differently. Equal training predictions need not mean equal predictions on new inputs.
ml-linear-regression.example: Model: y_hat = 1 + x. Data: (x,y) = (0,1), (2,5). Predictions: 1, 3. Residuals: 0, -2. L = (0^2 + (-2)^2)/4 = 1; MSE = 2.
ml-linear-regression.takeaway: Distinguish predictions, residuals, loss and weights. Check the loss normalization.

ml-gradient-descent.title: Gradient descent: updates and step size
ml-gradient-descent.body:
For half-MSE, a full-batch gradient averages over all examples. With r_i = b + w*x_i - y_i, the bias gradient is mean(r_i); the weight gradient is mean(r_i*x_i). Compute both at the old parameters, then update simultaneously: parameter_new = parameter - alpha*gradient.

In matrix form, L = ||X*theta-y||^2/(2n) and gradient = X^T(X*theta-y)/n. Rows are examples; a column of ones includes a bias. For L = (h/2)(theta-theta_star)^2, h > 0, error e = theta-theta_star updates as e_new = (1-alpha*h)e. All starts converge when 0 < alpha < 2/h. At the boundary, nonzero error cycles; above it, nonzero error grows. At the minimum, it stays zero.

For scalar least squares without a bias or penalty, replacing x by c*x (c != 0) multiplies curvature by c^2. Rescale the initial weight by 1/c and alpha by 1/c^2 to preserve predictions. This is not a universal rule for rescaling one column of a multi-feature model.
ml-gradient-descent.example: Loss: L(theta) = (theta-2)^2. Start: theta = 0, alpha = 1/4. Gradient: 2(0-2) = -4. Update: theta_new = 0 - (1/4)(-4) = 1. Loss falls from 4 to 1.
ml-gradient-descent.takeaway: Check the loss normalization. Subtract a gradient computed at the old parameters. Step size depends on curvature.

ml-gd-q07.title: Will it converge?
ml-gd-q07.statement:
Loss: L(theta) = 2(theta-3)^2.
Exact gradient descent: theta_0 = 0, fixed alpha = 1/2.
ml-gd-q07.explanation: The error multiplier is -1, so the error changes sign without shrinking. Starting at 0 gives 0, 6, 0, 6, ... . Convexity does not guarantee convergence for every step size. Starting exactly at 3 would stay there.

ml-gd-q08.title: Increase the step size
ml-gd-q08.statement:
Same loss: L(theta) = 2(theta-3)^2.
Exact gradient descent: theta_0 = 0, fixed alpha = 3/5.
ml-gd-q08.prompt: What happens to the distance from 3?
ml-gd-q08.explanation: The error multiplier is 1 - 12/5 = -7/5. Since its magnitude exceeds 1, the nonzero starting error alternates in sign and grows without bound. In contrast, alpha = 1/4 makes the multiplier zero and reaches 3 in one step.
